facts: AstroMLab 5 aims to create structured summaries from 400,000 astrophysics papers.
Yuan-Sen Ting is affiliated with The Ohio State University.
Alberto Accomazzi is associated with the Harvard-Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics.
Tirthankar Ghosal works at Oak Ridge National Laboratory.
The dataset comprises 408,590 astrophysics papers from arXiv covering the period from 1992 to July 2025.
It includes the extraction of 9,999 unique concepts with detailed descriptions.
The dataset contains 3.8 million paper-concept associations.
The concept vocabulary and embeddings are publicly available at https://github.com/tingyuansen/astro-ph_knowledge_graph.

The deployment of large language models (LLMs) as autonomous agents is advancing in materials science and chemistry. The authors propose organizing all astro-ph papers into structured summaries and concepts. The initiative resulted in a dataset of 408,590 papers. The dataset includes 9,999 unique concepts with semantic embeddings and structured summaries.
The chosen method for converting astrophysics PDFs to machine-readable text is OCR.
Nougat was initially used to convert PDFs to markdown format, requiring about 1 minute per paper on a V100 GPU.
The transition to Mathpix OCR API occurred in November 2024.
Inspections of Mathpix's output for approximately 50,000 papers showed no systematic errors affecting summary quality.
The summarization approach divides academic papers into approximately 10,000-character segments at section boundaries.
The compression system prioritizes retaining LaTeX formulas and excludes acknowledgments and references.
The entire summarization process for 408,590 papers cost over $50,000 in API fees.
Raw summaries are reorganized into seven semantic sections for enhanced analysis and knowledge representation.
The methodology aims to identify approximately 10 novel concepts per paper.
Each concept includes a concise name, a classification, and a detailed description.
The final vocabulary consists of 9,999 concepts after manual review.
The methodology emphasizes scrutiny when utilizing the dataset for specific applications.
The new vocabulary achieves complete coverage of all 408,590 papers.
The average number of concepts per paper in the new vocabulary is 9.4.
Traditional ADS keywords are author-supplied and lack systematic curation.
Concepts are shown to be superior to abstracts for discovery tasks.
The temporal analysis tracks the emergence and evolution of concepts over three decades.
A notable peak in concept emergence occurred in 2007 due to changes in arXiv's cross-listing policies.
The co-occurrence analysis uses the Ochiai coefficient to examine how concepts appear together in research papers.
There has been increased integration of computational methods and machine learning in astrophysics research in recent years.
The dataset includes all astro-ph papers from 1992 to July 2025.
It features a CSV of concept vocabulary with labels, names, classes, and descriptions.
The dataset provides a citation network with 1.67 million unique identifiers.
Concept embeddings were generated using text-embedding-3-large.
The dataset contains 408,590 astrophysics papers from arXiv spanning the years 1992 to 2025.
It includes 9,999 AI-generated concepts with detailed descriptions.
Temporal analysis indicates a rise in machine learning in astrophysics from 2015 to 2025.
All code and data processing pipelines related to the dataset are publicly available.
The summary presents a structured format for academic papers across six sections: Background, Motivation, Methodology, Results, Interpretation, and Implication.
USco1606-1935 is identified as a candidate low-mass binary system using 2MASS data.
The methodology included photometric and astrometric analysis to confirm the binary nature of USco1606-1935 A.
If confirmed as gravitationally bound, USco1606-1935 would be a rare example of a young multiple system with wide separations.
